ideas.hook: Everyone's locking in till December 31st. I think we picked the wrong finish line.
ideas.script: Everyone's locking in till December 31st. I think we picked the wrong finish line. [pause] Since September there's this trend called the Great Lock In. People take the last four months of the year to fix themselves. Gym, sleep, money. Before January even hits. And honestly, I love it. I'm trying to do it too. [pause] But here's what I noticed. For us, January isn't the real reset. Ramadan is. And it's expected around early February, depending on the moon. That's like three and a half months away. [pause] Think about it. Every year we hit Ramadan cold. First week we're dying at suhoor, can't focus in taraweeh, and the phone's still running our life. So what if this lock-in is the warm-up? [pause] Right now I'm trying three things. [fill in: your real three, e.g. Fajr on time, less screen time, one page of Quran a day]. Small. Boring. But by February they won't be new anymore. [pause] So I'm not locking in for January. I'm locking in for Ramadan. What's the one thing you want locked in before Ramadan? Drop it below and I'll check on you.

sources.title: BuzzFeed: The Great Lock In is taking over TikTok again (Sep 2026)
The National: Expected Ramadan 2027 start date

ideas.title: Lock in for Ramadan, not January
ideas.why: Rides the Great Lock In / winter arc trend (Sept–Dec 2026) and gives it a Muslim twist: Ramadan is expected around early Feb 2027, about 3.5 months away.

ideas.hook: There's a discipline habit that takes three days a month, and almost none of us do it.
ideas.script: There's a discipline habit that takes three days a month, and almost none of us do it. [pause] In Islam there's something called the white days. The 13th, 14th and 15th of every Islamic month. A lot of people fast them. And there's a hadith in Sahih Bukhari where Abu Hurairah said his close friend, the Prophet ﷺ, advised him to do three things: fast three days every month, pray two rak'ahs of Duha, and pray witr before sleeping. [pause] Three days. Not thirty. Three. [pause] And here's why I think it hits different for guys our age. We talk about discipline all day. Cold showers, 5am routines. But fasting is the original discipline training. You tell your body no, for Allah, when nobody's watching. [pause] This month's white days are basically right now, and the next ones land around late November. Check your local masjid's calendar. [fill in: be honest about whether you've done this before]. I'm going to try it next round. [pause] If you've never fasted outside Ramadan, try one day. Just one. Comment 'in' and let's do it together.

sources.title: Sahih al-Bukhari 1981 (fast three days each month, Duha, witr)
Hijri calendar: Jumada al-Awwal 1448 (Oct 12 – Nov 10, 2026)

ideas.script: This Sunday, your Fajr alarm is going to be wrong. [pause] November 1st, clocks fall back an hour here in Ontario. Sounds like a gift, right? Extra hour of sleep. [pause] But here's what happens to a lot of us every year. Fajr suddenly shows up an hour earlier on the clock. Isha's earlier too. And if your alarm is still set for the old time, you wake up, the sun's already up, and Fajr's gone. [pause] [fill in: if it's true, 'and honestly, that's happened to me before. Not because I didn't care. Because I didn't plan.'] [pause] So here's what I'm doing this week. I'm grabbing my masjid's new timetable for November. I'm resetting every alarm. And I'm using that extra hour Saturday night to actually sleep earlier, not scroll later. [pause] Because a clock change is the perfect excuse. And excuses are exactly what we're trying to get rid of this year. [pause] Tag the brother who's definitely missing Fajr on Sunday.

ideas.hook: More than half of Canadian guys our age are on social media over three hours a day.
ideas.script: More than half of Canadian guys our age are on social media over three hours a day. And yeah, I see the irony of telling you this on TikTok. [pause] This is from a survey by the Canadian Men's Health Foundation. Two thousand Canadian men. Fifty-three percent of guys 19 to 44 said they're on social media more than three hours a day. And the heavy users were more than twice as likely to report anxiety. [pause] Three hours a day is twenty-one hours a week. That's a part-time job we're not getting paid for. [pause] But here's the part that got me. Henoc Muamba, the ex-CFL player, said the real damage is comparison. We're measuring our normal life against everyone else's highlight reel. [pause] And honestly, we already have the fix for that. The Prophet ﷺ said look at those below you, not those above you, so you don't look down on Allah's blessings on you. That's in Sahih Muslim. [pause] My screen time right now is [fill in: your real number]. I'm trying to get it under [fill in]. Comment yours. Honest numbers only.

ideas.title: Two psychology studies that kill overthinking
ideas.hook: Two psychology studies that should make every guy stop overthinking.
ideas.why: 'Psychology facts about men' Shorts are running at 52x and 20.5x their channel averages this week. This gives the same list format with real, named studies and a confidence angle young guys can use.
ideas.script:
Two psychology studies that should make every guy stop overthinking. [pause] First one. Cornell, around the year 2000. Researchers had college students walk into a room wearing an embarrassing t-shirt, a Barry Manilow shirt. The students guessed about half the room noticed. The real number? Around a quarter. Psychologists call it the spotlight effect. You think everyone's watching you. They're not. They're busy worrying about themselves. [pause] The second one hit me harder. It's called the liking gap. In a 2018 study, people talked to a stranger, then guessed how much that person liked them. Over and over, they guessed too low. The other person liked them more than they thought. [pause] So put those two together. Nobody's watching you as closely as you think. And the people you do talk to probably like you more than you think. [pause] That gym you're scared to walk into. That conversation you keep putting off. That video you're scared to post. The only person judging you that hard is you. [pause] So which one are you overthinking right now? Tell me in the comments.

Suggested caption: The only person judging you that hard is you #fyppppppppppppppppppppppp #viral #fyp #psychology #overthinking

sources.title: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky (2000), The spotlight effect in social judgment, JPSP
Boothby et al. (2018), The liking gap in conversations, Psychological Science
Outlier: Male Psychology Facts (779K views, 52x)

ideas.title: Seneca's definition of broke
ideas.hook: Seneca said the poor man isn't the one with too little.
ideas.why: Stoic one-liners about desire and control are hitting 34x channel averages right now. This pairs a real Seneca quote with the loud budgeting trend, a money angle you can talk about without acting rich.
ideas.script:
Seneca said the poor man isn't the one with too little. [pause] And this was coming from one of the richest men in Rome. In a letter to his friend Lucilius, he wrote: 'It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.' [pause] Think about that. You could be making more than last year and still feel broke, because what you want keeps going up faster. New shoes, new fit, new phone, whatever you saw on your feed this morning. [pause] And I think our generation is starting to get it. There's a trend called loud budgeting. Instead of pretending, people just say it: nah, I'm not spending on that, I'm saving. A 2026 Bank of America study found 75% of Gen Z look for ways to spend less when they make plans. [pause] That's not being broke. That's being in control. The guy who needs less can't be pressured and can't be bought, and he's usually the one who ends up with options. [pause] So be honest. What's one thing you keep buying that you don't really need? Drop it below.

Suggested caption: Seneca figured out being broke 2,000 years ago #fyppppppppppppppppppppppp #viral #fyp #stoicism #moneymindset

sources.title: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 2 (Gummere translation)
Cayman Independent: Loud budgeting and Gen Z (BofA 2026 data)
Outlier: 'You become free the moment your desires stop controlling you' (34x)

ideas.title: When's the last time you checked on your boys?
ideas.hook: When's the last time you called one of your boys just to check on him?
ideas.why: The goodnight-call trend showed that male friendship content lands when it's funny and real. This ends on a challenge built to get comments, and comment-bait endings are what your 'comment down' videos already use.
ideas.script:
When's the last time you called one of your boys just to check on him? [pause] Not to ask for something. Not to make plans. Just, 'yo, how are you actually doing?' [pause] There was this trend where guys call their friends at night just to say goodnight. And the reactions are hilarious, because every single friend goes, 'bro... you good?' [pause] But think about why it's funny. It's funny because it's so rare. We talk to our boys every day about games, the gym, money, whatever. But almost never about how we're actually doing. [pause] Pew Research found 8% of Americans say they have no close friends at all. Think about how many guys are going through something right now and just sitting on it. [pause] Being strong isn't never needing anybody. It's being the guy your friends know they can call. And sometimes that means you call first. [pause] So here's the challenge. Text one of your boys tonight and ask how he's really doing. Then come back and tell me what he said.

Suggested caption: Call your boys. Not for anything. Just because. #fyppppppppppppppppppppppp #viral #fyp #brotherhood #mensmentalhealth

sources.title: Straight Arrow News: Viral goodnight calls show the softer side of masculinity (cites Pew 2023)

> Surah Ibrahim, verse seven. Allah says, 'If you are grateful, I will surely increase you.' [verify source]

*Delivery:* slower, calm, let the verse breathe

[pause]

**Scene 5 - Value (20-26s)**
> Grateful first. Then more. Not the other way round. I had it backwards for years.

*Delivery:* short lines, nod on 'backwards'

[pause]

**Scene 6 - Payoff / CTA (26-36s)**
> So now before I sleep I name one thing I'm thankful for. Out loud. Today it was [fill in: your real one]. What's yours?

*Delivery:* warm, smile a little on the last question

**Last line:** "So now before I sleep I name one thing I'm thankful for. Out loud. Today it was [fill in: your real one]. What's yours?" (ends on the question, no loop)

  - One verse made me realise I had gratitude completely backwards. (Curiosity loop)
  - If you're waiting to make it before you say alhamdulillah, watch this. (Call-out)

items.title: 61% of young men feel they have little control over their lives
items.creator: Institute for Family Studies survey of 2,000 men aged 18-29 (Aug 2026)
items.metric: 61% agree 'I often feel that I have little control over the things that happen to me'; 43% agree 'I am inclined to think that I am a failure'
items.whyItWorks: A fresh, real stat that hits the exact viewer you talk to, and it sets up Epictetus' 'what's in your control' idea perfectly. Stat-then-philosopher is the pattern behind the stoic outliers.

items.title: 72% of young men think who you know beats hard work

items.metric: 72% agree 'Who you know is more important than ability or hard work'; 84% still say they have ambitious plans
items.whyItWorks: A debate line built in: half your viewers agree, half get annoyed. Perfect for a money/career mindset video that ends on a comment question.

items.title: 59% of single young men hesitate to ask someone out

items.metric: 59% hesitate out of fear of rejection; 73% say it's harder to know what being a man means than 20-30 years ago
items.whyItWorks: Fear of rejection is a masculinity/relationships angle that doesn't need you to be a dating guru. Pairs with Seneca on fear. Saved for a later day.

items.title: You become free the moment your desires stop controlling you

brief.headline: Reach dropped since Oct 21: go short, on-niche, specific captions
brief.summary: Your videos sat around 700 views until Oct 21, and your last five all landed near 250, so reach dropped across the board rather than one hook missing. The lesson from your winners: stay 30-40s, stay on niche, and gratitude/faith reflections get your best like rate. Today's best idea is Epictetus' fix for feeling out of control, built on a fresh survey stat about guys our age.

review.headline: Views dropped from ~700 to ~250 since Oct 21
review.summary: Before Oct 21 almost every video you posted landed around 690-830 views; your last five judged posts (Oct 21-24) all sat at 246-301, so something changed at the account level, not just one bad hook. Your best ones were short (31-40s) and two of the top three were gratitude/faith reflections with specific captions. Off-niche posts (an AI tool tutorial, a UFC take) did 0.4x even before the drop.

winners.title: Gratitude reflection ('Comment down what else your thankful for', #allah)
winners.why: 36s faith-and-gratitude reflection posted Oct 13 with a comment-question caption. Only 1 comment though, so the bump came from watch time, not the CTA. I can't watch it, so I can't judge the opening line.

winners.title: Self-improvement talking video (#success #ai, Oct 8)
winners.why: 40s, generic 'Follow for more' caption, so the caption tells me nothing about the hook. Within noise of your ~700 floor; no strong signal.

winners.title: 'Always choose the right' reminder (#allah, Oct 9)
winners.why: 39s faith reminder with a 6.9% like rate (54 likes), more than double your usual ~3%. People who saw it liked it, which says the topic connects with your audience.

losers.title: 'Ts too hard' 2-second clip (Oct 5)
losers.why: A 2-second meme clip, not a talking video. Not a fair comparison, just an off-format post.

losers.title: Self-improvement talking video (Oct 21)
losers.why: 34s, 'Follow for more' caption. First video in the drop: four more after it all stayed at ~250-300 regardless of length (34-61s), which points to reach, not this one video's hook.

losers.title: Self-improvement talking video (Oct 23)
losers.why: 61s, one of your longest. Length may not have helped, but every post in this stretch did ~250, so the sample can't separate length from the drop.

patterns: Step change on Oct 21: 13 of 14 posts before it got 690-834 views; all 5 judged posts since got 246-301. Posting time didn't change (all 9-11pm Toronto), so it isn't timing.
Off-niche topics underperform even in good weeks: AI/Claude tutorial (259) and UFC/Topuria take (303) were your only two sub-400 posts before Oct 21.
Faith/gratitude reflections got the most likes per view (54 and 21 likes) and 2 of the top 3 spots.
Winners were 31-40s; your 57-64s posts never beat the median.
Most captions are the same 'Follow for more' line, so TikTok gets no keywords about the topic and I can't match videos to scripts.
doMore: Keep videos 30-40s; open with the payoff in the first 3 seconds
One faith/gratitude reflection every few days, it has your best like rate
Write a specific caption line about the topic (keywords), not 'Follow for more'
Stay on niche: discipline, mindset, philosophy, faith
stopDoing: Off-niche posts (AI tools, UFC takes) on this page
skillSuggestions: content-scripts: make the caption step mandatory: one specific keyword line about the topic, never 'Follow for more' (it's on 15 of your last 20 captions)
trend-ideas: drop AI/business and sports takes from this page's rotation; both did 0.4x of your median
content-scripts: cap default versions at 40s; none of your 57-64s posts beat your median
content-scripts: the 'references/hook-playbook.md' the skill tells me to read is missing from the skill folder; re-add it
NEW SKILL idea: a quick 'posted' log where you mark which script each upload used, so the reviewer can match hooks to results
